name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
title: Budgets and Allowable Costs
answer: Budgets and allowable costs in AI research grants cover the direct and indirect expenses that a sponsor will reimburse, from personnel salaries and fringe benefits to equipment, travel, materials, publication fees, and the compute and data storage that AI projects often require. The scope includes the rules that determine which costs are allowable, allocable, reasonable, and consistently treated, as set out in sponsor guidelines and federal cost principles. For AI work, this often means separating routine cloud usage from capital equipment, and justifying costs like GPU hours, dataset licenses, or annotation services. It also covers the lifecycle from proposal development through award management, including rebudgeting and closeout.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for budgets and allowable costs runs on institutional financial systems, sponsored programs offices, and sponsor portals such as Grants.gov, Research.gov, and eRA Commons. These systems hold the chart of accounts, effort reporting, and approval workflows that turn a proposal budget into an award and then into expense transactions. For AI projects, cloud billing dashboards and internal chargeback systems for high-performance computing are often the source of truth for compute costs. Cost tracking may also rely on time and effort systems, procurement records, and subaward monitoring tools.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of building a budget begins with a clear statement of the project's needs, which are then mapped to the sponsor's cost categories and checked against allowability rules. For AI research, this often involves estimating compute hours, storage volumes, data acquisition or annotation costs, and personnel effort for model development and evaluation. Budget justifications explain why each cost is necessary and how the estimate was derived, using vendor quotes, historical usage, or published rates. After award, the same categories guide rebudgeting requests, cost transfers, and no-cost extensions, all of which require documentation and sponsor approval where thresholds are met.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in budgets and allowable costs center on compliance with sponsor terms, federal cost principles, and institutional policies, with audit trails that show costs are allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Provenance matters: every expense needs a receipt, a purpose, and a link to the project, and effort certifications must match payroll. For AI projects, specific risks include cloud costs that exceed the awarded amount, data or model licenses that restrict use, and publication fees that may or may not be allowable. Disallowances, audit findings, and cost overruns can result when documentation is missing or when costs are charged inconsistently.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon for budgets and allowable costs is shaped by rising compute demands, which push funders to clarify how cloud credits, GPU time, and data storage can be budgeted and reimbursed. Institutions are investing in real-time cost tracking and automated compliance checks to reduce manual effort and catch overruns earlier. There is also movement toward standardizing data management and sharing costs, open access fees, and software licensing as explicit budget categories. As AI research becomes more resource-intensive, sponsors and institutions continue to adjust thresholds, indirect cost rates, and reporting requirements to match practice.
